text.p: Some might see it as the perfect opportunity to give up smoking: Marxist rebels take you hostage at a party, police besiege the building and when the last cigarette is gone, no one can get out to buy a fresh pack.
Help is at hand, though, for nicotine addicts among the 74 hostages being held at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima since Dec. 17.

"We are taking in cigarettes, both Western and Japanese," International Committee of the Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler told Reuters. "We are trying to help the hostages make it through the day, to ease their ordeal."
The Red Cross' supply of cigarettes to the hostages -- along with food, water and fresh clothes -- may have annoyed as many captives as it saved from withdrawal symptoms, however.
Non-smokers among the hostages insisted on establishing smoking and non-smoking areas, former captive Carlos Aquino Rodriguez said in a telephone interview.

"We asked ... that the smokers not smoke in the room we were in, that they go out into the corridor," said Aquino, who was released on Dec. 22. "The Japanese really smoked a lot, but they were all in a room together so it was not so bad."
More than a dozen Japanese businessmen and ambassador Morihisa Aoki are among the hostages still being held.
